newsitem.title: GERMANY: Jobs impact of German tax reform seen taking time.
newsitem.headline: Jobs impact of German tax reform seen taking time.

text.p: German analysts believe the government's planned tax reforms will have little or no immediate positive effect on the labour market, an official parliamentary gazette said on Thursday.

Economists and other private-sector analysts testified at parliament's finance committee that up to four years would be needed for such effects to be felt, said Heute im Bundestag, an official digest of the day's events.
All, however, said the government's tax measures were a step in the right direction.
The first phase of the tax reform, due to start in 1998, would cut taxes on corporate profits to 40 percent from 47 percent, and reduce the solidarity surcharge to 5.5 percent from 7.5 percent.
The committee will hold hearings on the second phase, due in 1999, on May 14-16.

The eight analysts who testified agreed that jobs creation is the main challenge facing German officials and society as a whole. Cutting the tax burden while simplifying the system -- the aims of the government's reform -- is also the correct way to proceed, they said.
But the DGB trade unions federation said many average wage earners could end up paying more taxes under the plan, particularly due to changed rules on shift-work and commuting.
Norbert Walter, chief economist of the Deutsche Bank, said deeper reforms had been impeded by special-interest groups such as the ADAC car-drivers' association, churches and unions.

An official from the American Chamber of Commerce said Germany could only hope to attract jobs-creating foreign investment if it could demonstrate to decision makers that investing in Germany could be profitable.
